5.2.b Art medium  

The artists of Collide@CERN are all interested in physics. Their choice of medium is 

technically sophisticated, often inspired by engineering or physics. Ranging from 

interventions with scientists to films about high-energy physics, all the artworks that 

were produced as a result of Collide@CERN were filtered through media that lend 

themselves to the context of CERN as a high-tech science institution. Technologically 

literate artists utilised modern media to communicate their ideas about CERN. Jobin’s 

dancers emulated the movement of particles, illustrating CERN’s work. Jan Peter’s 

interest in Einstein’s theory of relativity sent him hunting for historical material from the 

CERN archives, and he used the clips he found there to discuss matters of time as it 

related to the organisation. Decelière and Hänni wanted to explore how the analogue 

turned into the digital at CERN, a project that is still evolving and based on CERN’s 

own technological research. Julius von Bismarck became enthralled with ideas of 

control in particles, creating an artificial swinging motion for a hanging lamp with the 

help of CERN engineers. Bill Fontana listened to the LHC for days, recording the 



! 199!

sounds it made with CERN physicists. Ikeda explored data in quantum dimensions, 

drawing directly on CERN data. These men have some understanding of and interest in 

high-energy physics. Through their collaborations with scientists and engineers at CERN 

they become even more literate.  

While Collide@CERN claims to focus on the process rather than the outcome, 

the specification for artists’ chosen medium sets some limitations to applicants. The 

international residency is for digital arts, and the local strand has also engaged in multi-

media, high-tech art such as film, sound and data art. The connection to digital art is 

made through Ars Electronica, which co-organises and funds the international strand. 

The director of the digital art emporium, Stocker, has introduced all of the artists’ 

lectures at CERN. Furthermore, some of the winning artists were already in 

collaboration with Ars Electronica before applying to Collide@CERN. Von Bismarck 

won the Golden Nica award in 2008, and Ikeda in 2001. As the largest European festival 

dedicated to the intersections of art, technology and science, the Ars Electronica festival 

in Linz has likely interested many of the Arts@CERN artists at some point. Through Ars 

Electronica, CERN has reached out to a seasoned partner, which can provide a shortlist 

of artists and art projects already found appropriate. While countless artists have 

interacted with Ars Electronica over the years, the similar content of many of the 

artworks may be one of the reasons why the festival has not succeeded in penetrating the 

public consciousness. For example, the many dance projects at CERN all utilise the 

dancers’ bodies as particles, and many artists interested in sound and light explore this 

through recording the noises that come from the LHC. Respect and curiosity for both 

scientists and science ties all the Collide@CERN artists together, and this is expressed 

through their talks at CERN and the art inspired by their experiences there. In the still 

small and exclusive world of SciArt, Ars Electronica and its awards are comparable to 

the Oscars. It mirrors particle physics’ focus on media, celebrity and branding, and its 

insistence on competition and hierarchy as methodologies of finding both “excellent” 

artists and elusive particles.  

The chosen media of the Collide@CERN artists, usually dance, performance, 

sound art, film or installation, all lend themselves to a specific message. These live 

events and objects cannot be fixed to CERN as a sculpture or painting could. The 



! 200!

original dances, performances, interventions and sounds produced by the artists are now 

gone. They remain memories of matter and events, like the particle collisions recorded at 

CERN, a point often made in the lectures.21 These temporary spurs of creative energy at 

CERN are quick, fluid interventions that are observed live by relatively few people. The 

media attention about these events and objects live on for a wider audience to enjoy, 

alongside recorded clips of interviews and events authored by CERN through 

Arts@CERN. Thus the technologically savvy SciArt that the Collide@CERN artists 

create serves not only their interest in science and engineering, but also the quick pace of 

CERN PR and knowledge dissemination in the twenty-first century. The artists and art 

of Collide@CERN work in a temporary medium that is later disseminated through 

language and social media. The audience who is not present for the original event has to 

rely on these interpretations. The Collide@CERN artists’ choice of media results in a 

few original performances, followed by permanent ownership by CERN.

artists visited CERN for the first time. In many instances the artists and CERN wanted

5.4 Outcome of residency 

As the third of the five themes about the Collide@CERN artists, this section explores 

the various outcomes of the residency in subsections that relate to lectures, interventions, 

and artworks and networks respectively. This is done in order to examine the 

contemporary art programme at CERN, and how it relates to PR and the institutional 

nature of SciArt. Koek has made it clear that Arts@CERN is about “dropping a 

discipline into the unknown”, and that it is “not instrumentalising the science by using

5.4.a Lectures  

Each of the winning artists have so far given one lecture at the start and one at the end of 

their residency. These are presented in the Globe of Science and Innovation, a space 

dedicated to public engagement. The lectures introduce the science community at CERN 

to the artist and vice versa, although most of the artists already had a chance to explore 

the site in preliminary visits. Lectures were usually introduced by Director General 

Heuer, Ariane Koek, Stocker from Ars Electronica and the artist’s science inspiration 

partner. Heuer’s position as Director General continues to be important in securing a 

CERN audience and giving legitimacy to the event. In his opening addresses he 

accentuated how excited he and CERN were to host artists of excellent international 

reputation. Following him, Stocker introduces Ars Electronica and Koek introduces the 

artist. The lectures conclude with a moderated discussion and wine. The events were all 

streamed live, and later made available online.  

In March 2012 Julius von Bismarck described CERN as important and 

inspiring.43 He introduced his interest in the unexplained concept of: “hidden world 

things” and announced that he was interested in working on visibility at CERN. Von 

Bismarck answered my question about the reception of the project: “Many artists and 

scientists think SciArt is bullshit. But they should respect that not everyone is aware of 

it.” His defence of science enthused the audience, largely made up of scientists. “What 

happens”, he demanded, “if we call the scientist an artist, and the artist a scientist?”44 

Six months later Heuer stated: “Julius’s worldview is changed forever.”45 Before Koek 

introduced von Bismarck in his final lecture she reminded the audience that “…it’s all 

about the ideas generated, not the product but the generation of ideas…”46 This is at the 

core of the collaboration’s goals, and specifically relevant in the case of von Bismarck, 

as no new art was produced (his piece, Versuch unter Kreisen, was made during his time

5.4.b Interventions  

The Collide@CERN winners were expected to make interventions at the organisation. 

Jobin’s interventions included choreography where dancers performed in the CERN 

library. The interventions were not performances, but rather interactions with staff and 

the site. The dancers emulated particles, colliding, flipping over and between each other. 

In the early performances on-site, Jobin acted as a magnet that controlled the direction of 

their movements and rendered them chaotic when he moved around. The dancers, in 

brightly coloured clothing, underlined the different characteristics of each entity. They 

suggested a self-contained individuality that the magnet, however powerful, could not 

control. Likewise, the dancers were choreographed but also free to stop the dance or 

improvise. Dancers hung off of machines, twisted through library shelving and folded 

over furniture, resulting in high-resolution images that were disseminated online (Fig. 

42).

In the first of von Bismarck’s three interventions he locked thirty physicists 

underground and asked them what they saw in the complete darkness. Subdued inside 

CERN’s historical archives he wanted to start a discussion about how both the arts and 

the sciences are preoccupied with the concept of invisibility. Recognising his own 

shyness in many of the scientists, using darkness was one of the few ways that the artist 

felt comfortable to talk to what he called the “smarter people” at CERN.52 We should 

however keep in mind that von Bismarck often uses irony as part of his artistic oeuvre, 

so that his commentary might have been part of the intervention too. The following 

intervention that Bismarck provided was a ninety-minute art course to some of the staff. 

Confident in his knowledge outside of science, von Bismarck set about introducing the 

physicists and engineers at CERN to the art world. In subsequent public lectures he 

spent little time discussing this intervention, although this event was the only one in 

which a Collide@CERN artist taught scientists about art, rather than the other way

5.4.c Art and networks 

When the Collide@CERN artists use CERN as a studio and muse, they are encouraged 

to focus on learning, rather than production. Collide@CERN is not invested in making 

art. It is a system where the process, not the outcome, is key. This is why it is the figure 

of the artist, and not the role of art, that Ariane Koek and the programme emphasises: 

 

… it is stressed that the residency at CERN is all about research and 
discovering new ideas. CERN is a research centre after all. No outcomes 
are expected, although of course if they happen that is great. It is every 
tribute to CERN that the laboratory has embraced this idea – it is unusual 
for a science laboratory to have the foresight to give value to the creative 
research process rather than the outcome.58 

 

While the process takes priority for the Collide@CERN artists, the art also has a role to 

play. Artists are in part judged on their experiences of making art as the cultural board 

picks the residency winners. Furthermore, much is made of the artworks that are 

produced while the artist is at CERN. Finally, the artists’ post-CERN art production is 

included in the Arts@CERN canon. The following section discusses such artworks as 

one of the outcomes of the residency, analysing how this has benefitted CERN and the 

individual artists.

However, in the existing Collide@CERN artworks there are similarities. Inspired 

by engineering and high-energy physics theory, Quantum, Versuch unter Kreisen, The 

Universe of Sound and SuperSymmetry all perform science through artistic forms. 

Jobin’s dancers perform particle movements, von Bismarck’s lamps create false gravity, 

Fontana’s soundtrack is a sonic reading of the Large Hadron Collider, and Ikeda’s

present CERN to audiences traditionally beyond the reach of the organisation. 

Penetrating the worlds of contemporary dance, performance, sound art, social media and 

The Guardian art column, their projects introduce new audiences to CERN. 

Furthermore, they become commodities. Jobin, von Bismarck and Ikeda’s pieces in 

particular have become commercial entities, performances for sale on stages around the 

world (it has not been possible to find out if CERN profits from this).

5.6 Benefit to artists 

As each artist thanked CERN for the residency opportunity, they reflected on what they 

had gained from the interaction. They all gratefully acknowledged the chance to 

collaborate in an interesting space and with interesting people. Making contact with the 

arts professional Ariane Koek and their individual science inspiration partners was 

always important. While some confidence might have been lost along the way, the 

benefit of accepting the residency usually outweighed this. Gaining three months of 

work that was not tied to any outcome was seen as a rare opportunity. Likewise, there 

were financial benefits to winning the Collide@CERN residency. Each winning artist 

received 10,000 Euros in prize money (from anonymous donors), as well as cover for

of being an artist at CERN have, on a whole, never been bigger.   

 

5.7 Conclusion 

In this chapter I have explored the Collide@CERN artists, asking who they are, what 

experiences they have had at the organisation, what the work they made there means, 

and what benefits they gained from the residency. I have found that their time at CERN 

is not without conflict, but that it is usually a positive experience. Some artists created 

art as a direct consequence of spending time at CERN, and all of the winners gained 

access to networks, prizes, recognition and some financial stability post-CERN. While 



! 221!

most of the artists struggled with an inferiority complex in their interactions with 

scientists, many created warm working relationships with their science partners despite 

this.83 Selected from a pool of over 300 applicants, the artists were already filtered by 

CERN and found to be suitable matches for the organisation’s goals. Furthermore they 

(and other CERN artists) usually mirrored the demographic makeup of CERN staff in 

terms of their nationalities, their gender and the career stage that they were in. In the 

artists’ post-residency relationships with CERN they may also continue to benefit from 

the organisation’s networks. Having access to CERN gives individual artists access to 

certain networks and benefits. But in the controlled cultural atmosphere of the cultural 

board and residency application system, artists who are not invited to work with the 

organisation have little chance of visiting the site. While they may share a passion for 

science, these artists can now be excluded from CERN. So what is it like for the artist 

who does have CERN as a studio today? Under contract, freedom may be compromised, 

but there are also new opportunities, networks and benefits to explore. Furthermore, in a 

time where some art residencies ask artists to pay a fee, Collide@CERN treats artists as 

professionals.84 Gaining knowledge, friendships, funding and access to networks, 

Collide@CERN artists are as celebrated by the organisation as the organisation is 

celebrated by them.

CONCLUSION 

Boundary Breakers? Artists at CERN. 

 

In this thesis I asked why CERN is investing its resources in a structured art programme 

now. The answers presented reveal the institutional structure of SciArt through the case 

study of CERN. CERN has always had an active PR office, and branding and image 

have become integral to how it operates as a globally recognised organisation. CERN’s 

goal of legitimising its work as part of its survival strategy remains, and PR is crucial to 

sustaining this. CERN’s PR strategy has changed over the decades, but has only very 

recently included the arts and artists. This thesis has, for the first time, questioned these 

SciArt structures as features of promotional culture in science. In this conclusion I 

discuss the key findings that have been revealed from this analysis. I reflect on my 

methodology, revisit the key findings of the individual chapters, explore how this project 

expands various literatures, and discuss key themes. 

 

Reflections on methodology  

This thesis utilised interviews, archival research, site visits, art historical approaches, 

and theories of gender and cultural capital as part of its methodological framework. I 

used an inductive approach to interpret this data. This approach proved to be successful 

because it allowed me to understand the patterns and relationships between the 

economic, institutional and cultural factors that have created an art project at CERN 

today. While the textual sources and interviews provided rich contextual evidence to 

support the claims made in this thesis, as in all research, there are limitations regarding 

the researcher’s interpretations of the data. Nevertheless, using both primary and 

secondary data has provided a broad and unique understanding of arts at CERN, and of 

how scientific institutions such as CERN shape and control SciArt. 

 

Reflections on chapters 

The first chapter, ‘Image’, explored the historical use of PR and branding at CERN. I 

provided a scholarly investigation of CERN’s PR office, drawing on archival material 

and interviews. I used the case study of the ‘Higgs Boson Blues’ to find out how 



! 223!

CERN’s history of PR has informed its current Communication Group. I examined this 

through a close reading of the song’s lyrics. I also interviewed the current head of the PR 

office, James Gillies, and found that CERN as a rule differentiates between art and 

popular culture (although the exceptions to this reveals insight into other public 

engagement goals), and that it choses what it has time to engage with. I also explored the 

controversial issues that surround the organisation, in particular questions of gender and 

diversity, conspiracy theories, and financial pressures. Understanding these difficult 

topics explain why CERN needs PR today. The thesis shows that the Communication 

Group’s main task is to maintain CERN’s identity. But in the new post-Internet media 

landscape, the nature of PR is changing. I argue that art and artists are part of this change 

in PR at CERN, and that while they have agency, they do not have control over these 

structures. 

In the second chapter, ‘Contracted’, I explored SciArt and found that it lends 

itself to the goals of CERN’s PR office. Through examining the field of SciArt, and 

exploring how other physics laboratories have used the arts in the past, I argued that the 

institutional nature of this new genre is perfectly suited to CERN’s needs. I traced the 

start of SciArt back to the Wellcome Trust’s initiative in the ‘90s, and showed how, ever 

since, the field has always been tied to institutions and hierarchical structures. This is the 

first critical examination of the field and history of SciArt, in contrast to most SciArt 

literature that celebrates or explains the field. I argue that SciArt, like any genre of art, 

should be carefully examined, and that this includes investigating the financial and 

institutional factors that created it.  

The third chapter, ‘Pasts’, presented the history of CERN art. Drawing on 

archival research, interviews, visits to CERN and art historical analysis, I introduce the 

artworks at the organisation. This is the first time the organisation’s visual culture has 

been explored. I show how CERN’s art history is eclectic and varied, comparing works 

that celebrate the organisation with pieces that engage in controversial topics. Drawing 

on my work about the history of PR at CERN, I show how the organisation employs 

silencing strategies in cases of controversial art. This provides an important framework 

for understanding how contemporary artists are chosen for the new art residency, and 

how they might experience their time at CERN. The chapter also argues that CERN has 



! 224!

always inspired artists, and that it is only now that the organisation seeks to culturally 

capitalise on this creativity, and thus improve its image to prove its legitimacy and 

secure funding.  

In the fourth chapter, ‘Control’, I explore why CERN is seeking to culturally 

capitalise on art and artists since 2011. I explore the origin of Arts@CERN, examining 

the people and financial support that created the project. For this, I analysed the 

economic and historical factors behind the origins of the scheme. I also used historical 

methods to explore E.A.T. and CAVS, comparing these two early science and art 

schemes with Arts@CERN. CERN is unique in significant ways, but comparing its art 

programme to E.A.T. and CAVS shows how CERN has chosen to shape Arts@CERN 

today. The chapter also presents a close textual analysis of CERN’s new cultural policy, 

showing how the rhetoric of this text underlines the organisation’s attitude to the arts 

and to artists. 

In the final chapter, ‘Artists’, I focused on the artists’ experiences at CERN 

today. I explored what type of artists succeed in the new Collide@CERN residency 

competition in terms of demography, stage of career and art medium. I looked at the 

experiences they had whilst at CERN, and the outcomes they produced (lectures, 

interventions, art and networks). I analysed the artists’ statements about confidence and 

creativity whilst at CERN, showing how there was an inferiority complex at work in 

many cases. I argued that although the artists gained some funding, networks, 

opportunities and friendship from the exchange, it was CERN that gained most. Having 

explored how CERN’s strong culture of PR has worked since the start of the 

organisation, and how the office did not culturally capitalise on the many artistic 

projects that took place before Arts@CERN, we can see why, in a time of intense 

reputational and financial pressures, the Communication Group sought to capitalise on 

this free opportunity. CERN has not had any expenses throughout Arts@CERN, as the 

money comes from external donors. In this context I argue that although Arts@CERN 

provides genuine creative ‘collisions’ between artists and scientists, it is also a genuine 

PR opportunity. The latter is what structures both the organisation’s cultural policy and 

attitude towards the arts, and based on my research I believe that CERN’s own interests 

will always be privileged over those of individual artists. This questions the common 



! 225!

notion that artists should be free to be creative, showing how both SciArt and 

Arts@CERN use the stereotypes surrounding artists for their own gains. These themes 

and my findings are discussed in detail below. 

 

Reflections on literature  

In this thesis I utilised several fields of scholarship, bringing them together in new ways 

from an art historical perspective. While interdisciplinary research can be challenging, it 

can also strengthen a project. Drawing on art history, science history, science 

communication studies, branding theory, sociology, anthropology, social science and 

gender studies, I have situated CERN in an interdisciplinary and complex reality (these 

literatures are discussed and referenced in the literature review part of the introduction). 

Most scholarship on CERN has focused on its scientific work and its machines. Utilising 

interdisciplinary literatures, I have shown how CERN is not only about science; it is also 

a cultural, economic and political space.  

Each separate field of scholarship has provided rich context to this study of 

SciArt at CERN, and in turn this project has located some limitations in the individual 

scholarly fields, and sought to fill those gaps. Within art history, there are very few 

scholars who explore science. Most of those who do, engage with scientific theory or 

discoveries. In contrast, this thesis explores the visual culture of a scientific institution, 

drawing on art historical methodology. In the history of science, many scholars have 

explored the culture of science, but there has been little engagement with the visual 

culture of scientific organisations. This thesis explores the scientific history of CERN, 

but focuses on the history of PR and art at the organisation, rather than on scientific 

theories or machines. In science communication studies we have been shown evidence 

for the relationship between PR and science. This thesis expands this relationship to 

include artists, and shows how they are also part of the science communication network 

of contemporary science. Sociologists and anthropologists have long been interested in 

how scientists work. In this thesis I show how artists, as both non-scientists and 

professionals, experience a scientific organisation. I have explored how this clash of 

cultures functions as useful PR for CERN, and is at times complicated for the 

individuals involved. Gender studies and feminist science theory have explored the lack 



! 226!

of women in science, the forgotten women of the past, and the theoretical implications 

of inequality. In this thesis, I have shown that there is not only a lack of women at 

CERN, but also a lack of women in SciArt and Arts@CERN. I have argued that there 

needs to be a dedicated analysis of inequality in SciArt, and that the lack of diversity in 

Arts@CERN and Ars Electronica could start that conversation. I have also drawn on 

Bordieu’s ideas about cultural capital, expanding this to explore scientific capital and 

artistic capital at CERN. Thus, the project draws on several vast literatures, addressing 

limitations in these fields, and filling some gaps. Likewise, this work should be of 

interest to art historians who work on science, science historians, science communication 

scholars, sociologists and anthropologists of science, economists who explore science or 

art, and scholars who work on theories relating to science and art.  

 

Key findings 

This study is unique in its focus on the institutional history of SciArt. Artists experience 

CERN as non-scientists and creative observers, led through a series of initiation 

processes in order to produce desired outcomes for the organisation. These outcomes 

(whether art works, interventions, debate or other forms of cultural capital) benefit the 

organisation more than it does the individual scientists or artists involved in the 

programme. In the mid-‘90s, the pioneering SciArt programme initiated by the 

Wellcome Trust found that artists stood to gain more than scientists from collaboration.1 

In this thesis the focus has been redirected towards the institutional nature of the 

collaboration, the entity that is profiting most from SciArt. This is not to say that artists 

and scientists get nothing from the CERN art programme, but they are neither the 

catalysts nor main beneficiaries of its structure.  

A key issue explored in this thesis concerns how artists, in the course of their 

interaction with CERN, function both as non-scientists and professionals who lend their 

expertise to ‘sell’ CERN’s brand. Some artists have experiences of CERN that are 

similar to other non-scientist groups, not fully accessing the inner workings of the 

organisation, either because they do not wish to, or because they are not invited to. They

A further significant finding of this thesis centres on the outcomes of the art 

programme at CERN today. The focus of Arts@CERN is on collaboration and 

discussion, rather than on making art. There is no expectation that the artist will produce 

an artwork by the end of their residency. Nevertheless, as this thesis shows, CERN often 

holds artists to account after their residencies finish. The job of the artist can sometimes 

be to deepen the mystery of their host institution. In the current art programme at CERN, 

the creative participants have in part been brought in to do this job. In some cases, the 

direction established by their time at CERN continues to be followed after the residency

organisation to secure its future funding and existence.  

 To this end, artists are coopted to CERN’s branding strategy. Post-Higgs era 

CERN continues its work in the public sphere, often with the help of science museums, 

journalists, celebrities and individuals such as Ariane Koek. The exhibition Collider at 

the Science Museum is one example, as are CERN’s many public Twitter accounts, 

public speakers such as Brian Cox, and visiting celebrities such as Will.i.am. There was 

already SciArt activity at CERN prior to Ariane Koek’s arrival there, but it was not 

coordinated or publicised in a way that would reach people beyond the high-energy 

physics community and, more importantly, funders. Today, CERN has made culture part 

of its PR through utilising SciArt as public engagement. As an organisation dependent 

on public funding and being seen as legitimate, PR is part of its survival strategy. It is 

not surprising that CERN wants its SciArt to function as PR, and place their artists under 

contract. However, since CERN was founded 1954 it has wrestled with critics and 

conspiracy theories that have endangered its reputation, and thereby its survival. CERN 



! 230!

distribute its message through careful selection of artists. In the past, this was not done, 

and many artists produced conspiracy theories because the laboratory captured their 

imagination. Today, through the Arts@CERN structure, CERN can harness positive 

messages from handpicked artists, and exclude artists who do not comply with the 

organisation’s narrative. Thus, CERN is using cultural capital to communicate its 

importance to the outside world. Whether this strategy is beneficial or not will depend 

on how the public and funders view CERN in the future. After discovering the 

anticipated Higgs boson, it is not clear what happens next for CERN. In a situation based 

on public opinion and changing factors, the art programme at CERN is not necessarily 

safe from being cut in the future. But for now, Koek has shown that artists can be used 

in the organisation’s branding strategy through media coverage, and through the

world.

images.6 At CERN, some artists are a part of the trend within SciArt that embraces the

INTRODUCTION 
CULTURAL POLICY FOR ENGAGING WITH THE ARTS

This is CERN’s first cultural policy for engaging with the arts. It was conceived as the foundation 

for Collide@CERN – the International Artists Residency programme. It became quickly apparent 

that if there is to be an International Arts Residency scheme, CERN crucially needed a Cultural 

Policy for Engaging with the Arts to provide the essential policy framework and foundations for 

the Collide@CERN arts residency initiative, as well as for all other high quality arts engagement 

and activities. 

CERN's first cultural policy for engaging with the arts is called Great Arts for Great Science. 

Both arts and science are ways of exploring the world we live in and our place in the universe. 

Science demonstrates its effectiveness through tests, equations and proof thus creating new 

knowledge and certainty, the arts demonstrates its impact through the senses, transporting 

people to see the world and relate to each other with a sense of wonder through the power of the 

imagination. 

WHY GREAT ARTS FOR GREAT SCIENCE? 

Called Great Arts for Great Science, CERN`s cultural policy creates for the first time the 

essential foundation and framework at CERN for expertise and knowledge of the arts to 

match CERN`s world renown for expertise and knowledge in science. 

Great Science deserves Great Art – with the same high standards of selection and quality 

control that are made to employ talented world-class scientists, engineers and 

technologists at CERN, being matched by CERN selecting equally talented, world-class, 

innovative artists. The policy will enable this with a key recommendation, building in the 

necessary expertise by setting up for the first time an independent Cultural Advisory Board 
for engaging with the Arts (CABA). 

By adopting Great Arts for Great Science, CERN can clearly demonstrate to the global 

cultural community that it is a cultural force – by engaging its great science with great arts. 

2

Camilla Mork Rostvik
278



“GREAT” 
IS DEFINED AS... 

Established Talent – World-class and recognized excellence, exceptionalism and ability. 

Emerging Talent – New talent that demonstrates exceptionalism, innovation, imagination and 

the ability to break the mould in their art forms to create the truly original and inspirational. 

Whilst in science, greatness is measured according to the absolutes of scientific proof and 

results, in the arts it is judged and assessed according to a combination of the experience and 

knowledge of the history of the different art forms demonstrated by experts - who include 

practitioners, curators, directors, producers, and critics. These are the kinds of people qualified to 

make valued critical judgments and choices about artists and their quality, their exceptionalism 

and their ability – thus ensuring Great Art for Great Science. 

PLEASE NOTE:

The term ‘artists’ is used generically to encompass people who work in the fields of dance, 

literature, theatre, film and television, digital arts, visual arts, architecture, design and music – the 

entire range of artistic activity as it is defined in the outside world.

THE FOUR MAIN STRATEGIES 
FOR GREAT ARTS FOR GREAT SCIENCE 

The following four strategies are essential for ensuring that the aims, values, and missions of 

Great Arts for Great Science are implemented in the Cultural Policy: 

STRATEGY ONE 

To create expert knowledge in the arts, in addition to that provided by an arts professional, by 

setting up the honorary Cultural Advisory Board for engaging with the Arts (CABA) that will include 

arts professionals at the highest level. 

STRATEGY TWO 

To create clear entry points for artists to visit CERN in which CERN adopts a system for dealing 

with unsolicited cultural proposals and artists enquiries, including visits, with a single point of 

contact, an arts professional, who has cultural expertise and knowledge to evaluate the requests. 

The arts professional works with the Cultural Advisory Board for Engaging with the Arts when 

major partnership proposals are made. The most obvious and clear entry point for artists will be 

the Collide@CERN Arts Residency Programme. 

STRATEGY THREE 

To instigate Collide@CERN the arts residency scheme to encourage dialogue and exchange 

between arts and science at the same level by selecting imaginative and extraordinary artists for 

their excellence to work alongside CERN scientists. 

STRATEGY FOUR 

To provide for the first time professional cultural expertise and advice to already existing 

homegrown arts activities at CERN – CinéGlobe, for example – to enable them to fulfill their 

cultural potential.

abstracts.value: This thesis explores the historical and contemporary practices of cultural engagement and management at the European Organisation for Nuclear Research (CERN). It considers the history of art at CERN, and the role of the artists who have engaged with the organisation. Furthermore, it traces CERN's history from the beginning of the organisation in 1954 to the contemporary art programme Arts@CERN, including the artist-in-residency competition Collide@CERN (both initiated in 2011). Approaching the topic from an interdisciplinary angle, the thesis utilises art history, science history, critical studies of branding and public relations, science communication and various theoretical disciplines in order to understand why selected artists are being invited to collaborate with CERN today. My original contribution to knowledge is a case study showing the institutional nature of SciArt (an art genre that combines art and science) at CERN, connecting this to the institutional use of art and artists as public relations.

titles.title: At the Edge of their Universe: Artists, Scientists and Outsiders at CERN

abstracts.value: Quantum batteries (QBs) represent a promising and emerging class of energy storage devices that exploit the principles of quantum mechanics to achieve superior performance compared to conventional, classical batteries. In this work, we investigate the charging dynamics of a QB in a bipartite system composed of two qubits, where one qubit acts as a charger and the other as the battery, each embedded in an independent cavity reservoir. The model incorporates multiphoton atom-cavity interactions as well as quenched disorder (QD) in the system-reservoir coupling, including discrete, uniform, Gaussian, and Cauchy-Lorentz distributions. The resulting dynamics are analyzed in both weak- and strong-coupling regimes. We examine how the multiphoton order affects the internal energies of the charger and the battery, and show that increasing the multiphoton order leads to enhanced dissipation and a reduction of the energy transferred to the battery. By comparing different disorder statistics, we find that uniform and discrete QDs can partially mitigate decoherence and yield higher charging efficiency compared to Gaussian and Cauchy-Lorentz QDs. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that strong system-reservoir coupling induces non-Markovian dynamics accompanied by rapid energy loss and suppression of ergotropy and efficiency. In contrast, efficient charging and partial revival features are predominantly observed in the weak-coupling, Markovian regime, where coherent dynamics are preserved.

titles.title: Impact of quenched disorder and multiphoton interaction on the dynamics of a quantum battery

abstracts.value: Job scheduling is an NP-hard optimization problem with clear industrial relevance. In practice, distributing work across a team is not only about meeting deadlines or improving productivity; it also affects fatigue, stress, and employee well-being. Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) provide a promising way to address these problems through QUBO formulations, although their scalability on near-term NISQ hardware is still limited by Hilbert-space growth and barren plateaus. In this work, we simulate a VQA for a realistic Multi-Skill Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (MS-RCPSP), including worker capacities, skill matrices, task priorities, deadlines, and calendar stability during rescheduling. To keep the problem within a near-term circuit size, we use a temporal batch decomposition that solves one day at a time, propagates the remaining workload, and combines it with a logarithmic binary encoding that keeps every batch at or below 30 qubits. Because the ground state of a QUBO Hamiltonian is a computational basis state, entanglement is not required to represent the solution, raising the question of whether it helps or hinders ansatz training. We address this question by comparing the linear and brick-wall entangling topologies of a hardware-efficient ansatz with an entanglement-free reference that has the same number of parameters and by training every configuration with COBYLA and with Adam using SPSA gradient estimation. For the instance and initialization studied, the entanglement-free reference produced feasible schedules under both optimizers. With COBYLA, it produced the feasible schedule closest to the required workload at a fraction of the simulation cost of the entangled topologies, indicating that entanglement did not improve the solutions found by the VQA.

titles.title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Multi-Skill Project Scheduling

abstracts.value: We discuss a model of a soft waveguide described by Schrödinger operator whose potential is a twisted straight channel of non-circular profile. We show that a compactly supported twist makes the operator subcritical, the property being expressed in terms of a Hardy-type inequality. On the other hand, a periodic twist raises the essential spectrum and its local slowdown may give rise to isolated eigenvalues below the essential spectrum threshold.

abstracts.value: The spectral gap, the energy separating the ground state from the first excitation, governs many quantum phenomena, yet it is far harder to compute than the ground state. We propose a mathematically rigorous method for extracting the gap from imaginary-time evolution in infinite-dimensional Hamiltonians, where the first excitation typically marks the edge of a continuous spectrum. We show that a gap is not automatically detected: detection depends on how the initial state and observable couple the ground state to excitations at the bottom of the continuum. When this coupling follows a power law, the gap is recovered together with a logarithmic correction whose coefficient yields the exponent of the spectral density near the edge of the continuum, which reflects the physics of the excitations. We confirm both predictions numerically for an exactly solvable model. Our results offer a new numerical approach to many-body quantum physics, in which both the gap and the threshold exponent are obtained merely at the cost of a ground-state calculation.

titles.title: Beyond the Gap: What Imaginary-Time Evolution Reveals About the Edge of the Continuum

abstracts.value: We reformulate two-dimensional conformal field theory (2d CFT) in the language of noncommutative geometry. To this end, we introduce automorphic forms for the von Neumann algebraic quantum group $\mathrm{SL}^+_b(2,\mathbb{R})$. A quantum measure space is a von Neumann algebra equipped with a weight. We study such spaces carrying a weight-preserving action of $\mathrm{SL}^+_b(2,\mathbb{R})$. We argue that every unitary bosonic 2d CFT with central charge $c=1+6(b+b^{-1})^2>1$ is equivalent to a quantum measure space with an action of $\mathrm{SL}^+_b(2,\mathbb{R})\times\mathrm{SL}^+_b(2,\mathbb{R})$. In this dictionary, Virasoro primary operators are quantum automorphic forms and their scaling dimensions correspond to the spectrum of a quantum Laplace operator. The Virasoro crossing equations express associativity of multiplication on the quantum measure space. For compact theories, the algebra is a type III$_1$ factor. Liouville CFT is realized as $\mathrm{SL}^+_b(2,\mathbb{R})$ acting on itself by left and right translations. abstracts.value: Erasures are used to model faults at a subset of known locations in various platforms used to construct fault-tolerant quantum computers. Classical expander codes, which belong to the family of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, can be equipped with the Peeling decoder which works in linear time. Our main result is the algorithm Small-Set-Peeling, a quantum generalization of the classical Peeling decoder for erasures, that applies to quantum expander codes (Tillich, Zémor, IEEE T-IT 2013; Leverrier, Tillich, Zémor, FOCS 2015). abstracts.value: Mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) describe complementary quantum measurements: certainty in one basis gives no information about the others. In dimension six, triples of MUBs are known, but whether a fourth basis could exist remained unresolved for over three decades. OpenAI recently reported a proof that none exists. Here we use the topology of the space of complex Hadamard matrices, which describe transitions between MUBs, to characterize all sets in dimension six. We prove that every mutually unbiased triple belongs to a two-parameter family or is a single isolated triple built from the Fourier matrix. Since none of them extend to a fourth basis, this also proves that no four MUBs exist. Our proof rests on a new topological result that all order-six complex Hadamard matrices except Tao's form a connected space. Connectedness reduces the classification of triples to finitely many overlapping four-dimensional phase balls. We certify with interval arithmetic that these balls cover the space and for every pair of MUBs represented in a ball, we then determine all third bases that extend it. Dimension six is now the first non-prime-power dimension in which all sets of MUBs are classified.

titles.title: Using topology to reveal all mutually unbiased bases in dimension six

abstracts.value: In quantum many-body physics and quantum field theory, it is often assumed that gapped systems remain gapped under sufficiently weak local perturbations. However, to what extent this assumption holds is elusive, except for some special systems. In this work, we examine the stability of energy gap of macroscopic quantum matter that is only subject to two physically natural conditions, locality and translation invariance. We first show that in any spatial dimension, there are gapped local Hamiltonians with a unique ground state and an unstable gap, i.e., they become gapless under certain arbitrarily weak local perturbation in the thermodynamic limit. We then prove that for both spin and fermionic systems in one dimension, such Hamiltonians with an unstable gap must not only break translation invariance but also be fine-tuned. We further show that in any dimension greater than one, there are fine-tuned local translation invariant Hamiltonians with a unique ground state and an unstable gap. These results greatly sharpen our understanding of the fundamental problem of the stability of quantum phases of matter. We also discuss implications of our results on, for example, anyon superconductivity and higher-form symmetries.

titles.title: Stability of energy gap of macroscopic quantum matter

abstracts.value: Quantum-inspired numerical methods for partial differential equations represent discretized fields and operators as quantics tensor trains (QTT), so that their cost depends on how compressible the problem is rather than on the number of unknowns. We introduce a QTT Chebyshev--Galerkin method that assembles and solves global spectral systems directly in compressed form, without forming the underlying arrays. Starting from the weak formulation, the method handles coupled elliptic systems with variable coefficients, smoothly mapped geometries, and mixed Dirichlet--Robin boundary conditions, and yields symmetric positive-definite systems suited to variational tensor-network solvers. Parameters and random inputs enter as additional coordinates, so the same construction returns the solution over an entire parameter space in a single solve. In linear elasticity, the method retains spectral convergence and reaches errors below $10^{-8}$ on a three-dimensional benchmark, beyond those attained by QTT finite differences and Q2/Q4 FEniCSx finite elements over the tested range. abstracts.value: We study magnetic Bloch eigenvalue problems for two-dimensional magnetic Schrödinger operators with nonuniform periodic magnetic fields and periodic scalar potentials, and develop a hybrid Fourier-finite difference discretization. A Landau-type gauge is constructed by solving a periodic Poisson equation. Under the integer magnetic flux condition, the magnetic Bloch boundary conditions are incorporated through shifts of Fourier-mode indices. The method combines link-variable-based covariant central differences in the $x$-direction with a Fourier pseudospectral discretization in the $y$-direction, yielding a Hermitian discrete Hamiltonian. The resulting eigenvalue problems are solved using a LOBPCG method. Under appropriate regularity assumptions, we establish a fully discrete consistency residual estimate of order $O(h_1^2+N_2^{-s})$. With suitable spectral separation and eigenspace dimension-preserving conditions, error estimates of the same order are derived for isolated eigenvalues and their associated eigenspaces. Numerical experiments show second-order convergence in the finite difference direction and rapid error reduction with increasing Fourier resolution, and illustrate band degeneracies and eigenstate distributions in nonuniform periodic magnetic fields.

abstracts.value: Cosmic strings are one-dimensional topological defects formed during phase transitions in the early universe. ''Massive'' cosmic strings possess a sufficiently large tension to close their transverse space, forming a conical singularity outside the string, as a static gravitational effect. In a dynamical context, such strings are expected to drive topological inflation. In this work, we investigate the spacetime evolution induced by the formation of a massive cosmic string in a radiation-dominated cosmological background, imposing cylindrical symmetry. Using full numerical relativity simulations, we observe that the string core undergoes topological inflation and that its boundary moves inwards superluminally, which causally disconnects the core from the outer universe. Between the core and the asymptotic regions, a nearly matter-dominated decelerating region originates sourced by the oscillating string fields. This region is bounded by a local maximum (''belly'') and local minimum (''throat'') of the circumferential radius, while the throat recedes outwards at about 10% the speed of light. Furthermore, a gravitational wavefront is emitted from the string, characterizing the light cone of the string formation. Even behind the wavefront, the exterior region no longer exhibits a ''conical'' structure. Based on the simulation results, we construct a Penrose diagram, reflecting the causal structure of the entire spacetime.

abstracts.value: The two-body density matrix (TBDM) of a quantum many-body system provides information about particle correlations, e.g., pairing. In this work, we derive the complete spectrum of the TBDM of the fermionic Tonks-Girardeau gas using its exact ground-state wavefunction in second quantization. We obtain analytical expressions for all eigenvalues and eigenvectors for an arbitrary number of particles and identify two different types of eigenstates: collective states, formed by superpositions of paired momentum modes, and single-determinant states. We provide a physical interpretation of this structure, explaining the origin of the different eigenstates and their degeneracies. We further derive an asymptotic expansion for the largest eigenvalue, improving on previous estimates and analytically confirming its linear scaling with the particle number, thereby indicating off-diagonal long-range order. For the high-index collective states, we obtain simpler expressions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, showing that the eigenvalues decay as $n^{-4}$ and that the eigenvectors become independent of the number of particles. Finally, we discuss the connection between the collective states and an effective description in terms of composite bosons, whose spectral properties suggest a behavior consistent with Tan's contact for interacting bosonic systems.

abstracts.value: The abundance of compact objects ranging from stellar to intermediate masses ($\sim 1 - 10^{5}M_{\odot}$) remains poorly constrained, particularly for populations such as primordial black holes and dark matter subhalos that emit little or no electromagnetic radiation. Using simulated microlensed GW signals drawn from a realistic binary black hole population, we find that $\sim 100$ detected microlensed events are able to constrain both $α_{\rm ML}$ and $n_0$, although a degeneracy between the two remains. For a low-mass-dominated lens population ($α_{\rm ML}=2$) with $n_0=10^6~\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, a three-year observation at the O4 sensitivity yields $\sim 130$ detectable microlensed events and recovers the injected dark-matter fraction, $f_{\rm DM}\simeq 1.2 \times 10^{-4}$, with a 90% credible interval of $7.3 \times 10^{-5} \lesssim f_{\rm DM} \lesssim 1.8 \times 10^{-4}$.

abstracts.value: In quantum property estimation, an experimenter estimates $\operatorname{Tr}(Oρ)$ for a family of observables from independent copies of an unknown state $ρ$ simultaneously to additive error $ε$. While quantum memory can dramatically reduce sample complexity, understanding the power of a modest register that remains coherent throughout an adaptive experiment has remained an open challenge because existing frameworks require optimizing over the infinite space of measurement trees. We overcome this barrier by developing a backward-induction framework based on operator resolvents. Rather than tracking path-dependent memory states across rounds, resolvent regularization cancels internal memory trajectories exactly, reducing the lower bound to an algebraic certificate computed directly from the target observables with sharp $Ω(1/ε^2)$ scaling. Our structural rule charges only the retained dimension $K$ under arbitrary adaptive instruments and unrestricted memory lifetime. Via symmetry reductions, it yields polynomial-size linear programs that establish the optimal linear $Ω(D/(Kε^2))$ trade-off for the $D^2-1$ Paulis, eliminating the cubic loss in prior bounds. For growing weight-$w$ Pauli strings ($w=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$) and quadratic Majorana cross-correlations, it proves lower bounds of $Ω(3^w/ε^2)$ and $Ω(n^2/(ε^2(1+\ln n)^2))$ against an indefinitely persistent memory of dimension $K=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. These bounds match memoryless or commuting estimators within polylogarithmic factors, demonstrating that rank constraints on the persistent register fundamentally throttle observable overlap and prevent a modest coherent memory from overcoming the sample complexity barrier.

abstracts.value: We investigate nonequilibrium coherence spreading in quenched homogeneous bosonic gases both analytically and numerically. Our ensemble-averaged Gross-Pitaevskii trajectory approach and kinetic analysis confirm the linear-in-time growth of the squared coherence length, and explicitly give the spreading-law dependence on the ratio of initial energy to healing energy. abstracts.value: Driven-dissipative polariton networks offer a powerful analog platform for simulating continuous-spin Hamiltonians. However, their practical scalability is fundamentally limited by amplitude-phase coupling and metastable trapping in highly frustrated energy landscapes. Here, we present an \textit{in situ} dual-enhancement mechanism to address these bottlenecks without requiring external site-specific fine-tuning. First, a renormalization-group analysis based on density rescaling shows that higher-order nonlinear loss drives the condensates toward an incompressible regime, intrinsically suppressing amplitude fluctuations and enforcing phase-only dynamics. For macroscopic XY networks (up to 10,000 spins), this phase-amplitude decoupling yields a more than 50-fold reduction in energy, while simultaneously shrinking the standard deviation by a factor of six. More generally, it restores the extensive scaling of the optimized XY energy with system size. Second, to navigate the rugged, nonconvex energy landscape, we introduce weak Hermitian pulses. When implemented through a multistage protocol, these pulses enable repeated escapes from local minima and drive the system to deeper energy minima. Benchmarking shows an increasing advantage with system size, with the polariton simulator outperforming the classical Monte Carlo-SQP baseline in every sampled macroscopic realization. Our work provides a physical framework for scalable polariton analog computing.

abstracts.value: Fermionic teleportation near a Schwarzschild horizon involves two physically distinct ingredients that are often varied together: Hawking thermal mixing and the relative composition of the right and left Unruh modes. The solution yields a necessary-and-sufficient activation boundary, a second exact boundary for attaining the universal optimum, and explicit optimizing states. The resulting phase diagram contains a strict no-go region, a composition-limited activation region, and a universal-bound region. abstracts.value: Extended TeV gamma-ray halos around pulsars are commonly interpreted as evidence for slow diffusion of high-energy electrons and positrons near their sources, with diffusion coefficients about two orders of magnitude below the Galactic average inferred from B/C measurements. abstracts.value: Observed populations of rotating neutron stars~(NSs) with millisecond-order periods are powerful probes of fundamental physics. Mass-radius measurements inform poorly constrained properties of degenerate nuclear matter, whereas high-fidelity population synthesis connects unknowns in NS formation and binary evolution to large radio-timing surveys. However, repeated structure calculations are prohibitive due to the computational cost of solving the highly coupled partial differential equations of axisymmetric general relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium that govern rotating NS interiors. Non-rotating calculations or approximate rotational corrections can bias equation of state inference and limit the fidelity of population synthesis in tracing the evolutionary history of progenitors and propagating equation of state uncertainties. In this \textit{Letter}, we develop physics-informed neural operators that can solve the axisymmetric problem with high accuracy and negligible computational cost. \textit{Our solvers are trained in a fully unsupervised setting, with the training objective informed solely by the partial differential equations, and achieve a $10^3\times$ speed-up with negligible accuracy loss}. These solvers enable scalable EoS inference that self-consistently accounts for rotation and repeated stellar-structure calculations during binary evolution, making spin predictions that account for rotational structure and EoS uncertainties computationally accessible to population synthesis.

titles.title: Unsupervised Neural Operators for Rotating Relativistic Stars: High-Fidelity Equation of State Inference and Pulsar Spin Evolution at Scale

abstracts.value: Two-message quantum key exchange (2QKE) cannot be realized in a statistically secure way, and therefore some computational assumptions are required. So far, the known weakest assumption for 2QKE is the existence of one-way functions (OWFs). Can we construct 2QKE from a weaker assumption than OWFs? In this paper, we give the first complete characterization of 2QKE. We show that the following four primitives are (existentially) equivalent: everlasting-secure 2QKE, standard 2QKE, efficiently-verifiable state puzzles (EV-StatePuzzs), and one-time secure digital signatures with quantum signatures and signing keys. Because EV-StatePuzzs are potentially weaker than OWFs [Kretschmer, Qian and Tal 2025], the equivalence implies that 2QKE are potentially weaker than OWFs. Moreover, our result shows the equivalence between standard 2QKE and everlasting-secure 2QKE, which means that everlasting security comes for free. Finally, one-shot signatures, quantum lightning, and public-key quantum money mini-schemes imply EV-StatePuzzs, and therefore, our result also gives a new lowerbound, namely everlasting-secure 2QKE, of these public-key unclonable primitives. We also show that one-shot signatures imply QPKE with quantum public keys. [Kitagawa, Morimae,Nishimaki and Yamakawa, 2024] constructed QPKE with quantum public keys from OWFs, and it was open whether QPKE with quantum public keys can be constructed from an assumption weaker than or incomparable to OWFs. Our result gives a potential answer to this question since one-shot signatures seem to be incomparable with OWFs. Moreover, QPKE constructed from one-shot signatures has an additional functionality, which we call certified freeze, that allows the receiver to publish a publicly verifiable classical certificate that computationally binds the receiver to an upper bound on the total number of distinct valid ciphertexts under its verification key.

titles.title: Quantum Key Exchange from Public Quantum Money

abstracts.value: Quantum numbers associated with symmetries classify quantum states and identify the sectors relevant to a given simulation. Generic hardware-efficient ansatzes do not necessarily preserve the quantum numbers and may therefore explore states outside the target sector. We develop symmetry-guided algorithms based on the quantum-accessible Hilbert--Schmidt asymmetry (\(\AHS\)), which quantifies the deviation of a quantum state from invariance under a specified symmetry group. This quantity guides the optimization toward a highly reduced symmetry-based target sector, without enforcing the symmetry on the preparation circuit. We demonstrate the approach as a proof of principle in variational quantum eigensolver calculations targeting singlet ground states with collective SU(2) symmetry. The applications include a five-qubit \(S\)-wave \(p+{}^3\mathrm{He}\) two-cluster Hamiltonian, deduced from \textit{ab initio} many-body calculations, and collective spin models with up to 12 particles, which provide a many-particle benchmark of asymmetry-guided optimization. Across these applications, \(\AHS\)-based guidance increases the singlet probability. Overall, the proposed algorithms improve energy accuracy during optimization and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization, with substantial fidelity improvements in the larger spin systems. These results demonstrate the utility of an asymmetry objective determined by the group action, independently of the Hamiltonian energy, for improving the reliability of variational quantum optimization.

titles.title: Symmetry-guided algorithms for variational quantum optimization

abstracts.value: Bright coherent X-rays in the $\gtrsim$50 keV range are highly desirable for applications in materials science, high-energy-density physics, and nuclear physics, but are difficult to obtain from present X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) facilities. Plasma-based afterburners offer a compact route to increasing the electron-beam energy, yet high transformer ratio (TR) operation is vulnerable to hosing instability, which can severely degrade the witness beam quality. We propose using a transversely elliptical driver beam to excite an elliptical nonlinear plasma wake with an axially varying focusing gradient, thereby suppressing the witness beam hosing through betatron decoherence. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations show that, for a 3 kA driver and a 2.35 kA witness beam with an rms length of 4 $\mathrmμ$m and a beam separation of 94 $\mathrmμ$m (TR $\approx 3$), this scheme can accelerate an 8 GeV witness beam to $\sim30$ GeV while nearly half of the electrons meet the XFEL requirements. Start-to-end simulations show that the resulting beam can drive $\gtrsim50$ keV XFEL radiation with peak powers of $\sim10$ GW and durations of $\sim10$ fs, even when quantum diffusion is included, offering a compact route to extend existing XFEL facilities to higher photon energies.

abstracts.value: Perfectly matching local outcomes need not constitute a nondisturbing shared classical record. For finite-dimensional multipartite states, we prove that nontrivial exact records are equivalent to a spectrum sharing structure with a unique finest decomposition into locally distinguishable sectors, where entanglement may persist. For a fixed complete pointer, exact sharing is equivalent to strong quantum Darwinism together with global nondisturbance, while spectrum broadcast structure additionally requires conditional independence. Arbitrarily weak full-rank admixtures eliminate exact sharing, but two-sided distance bounds quantify robustness through disturbance and disagreement, while information bounds connect accurate local readouts to observer consensus.

abstracts.value: Very high energy electron (VHEE) beams offer several promising properties for radiotherapy. Accurate beam delivery requires a beam model that accounts for scattering along the beam propagation path. This work develops and validates a beam model incorporating Multiple Coulomb Scattering (MCS) to estimate beam parameters. MCS is incorporated as an additive term to the covariance matrix transformation for a drift space, allowing conventional quadrupole scans to estimate beam parameters in the presence of a downstream scatterer. The scattering correction factor is fitted to Monte Carlo (MC) simulations for a range of materials and thicknesses. The model is then validated by recovering the initial beam parameters from simulated quadrupole scans of a realistic beamline. Finally, the method is applied to in-air screen measurements at the Pulsed Energetic Electrons for Research (PEER) end station of the Australian Synchrotron. After fitting the correction factors, the mean and standard deviation of the estimation errors for the final emittance, diameter, divergence, and mean kinetic energy were $(-0.06 \pm 3.17)\%$, $(0.15 \pm 0.66)\%$, $(0.18 \pm 2.18)\%$, and $(-0.03 \pm 0.06)\%$, respectively. Simulated quadrupole scans successfully recovered the initial beam parameters, with errors of at most $13\%$. PEER measurements yielded emittance estimates ranging from $0.238$ to $1.753~\mathrm{mm\,mrad}$ across scans, which were within the expected range. Following an initial quadrupole scan, the method allows the in-air beam size to be estimated for other quadrupole configurations. Further work is required to improve the consistency and reliability of the experimental estimates.

titles.title: Estimation of Very High Energy Electron (VHEE) beam parameters using an in-air screen

abstracts.value: On-shell subtraction is a relevant step in finite-volume analyses, which is to isolate an on-shell singularity and evaluate regular momentum-dependent factors at their on-shell values. For short-range interactions with a finite mass gap, the correction associated with this on-shell subtraction is exponentially suppressed at sufficiently large volume and can therefore be neglected at the corresponding accuracy. We examine how this correction changes as the relevant mass parameter decreases. Using a common dimensional-regularization prescription, we derive analytic expressions for the resulting finite volume correction for representative momentum structures and examine their behavior numerically. For a nonzero mass parameter, the corrections are indeed exponentially suppressed at large $μL$, whereas in the massless limit this suppression is replaced by an enhanced finite-volume dependence. More importantly, the $S$-wave contribution can develop an infrared divergence of finite volume correction in the massless limit. These results clarify the conditions under which on-shell subtraction can be applied and provide guidance for assessing such corrections in finite-volume hadronic calculations involving long-range effects, including QCD+QED.

titles.title: Finite-volume Analysis of On-shell Subtraction in the Luescher formalism

abstracts.value: We study the low-temperature phase diagrams of $Spin(N)/SO(N)_\pm$ Yang-Mills theories as functions of the $θ$-parameter. In particular, for every even integer $N\geq 4$, we find a phase diagram consistent with the center/CP mixed anomaly, via the technique of mixed gauge theory. The resulting phase diagrams are in perfect agreement with the phase diagrams of $Spin(N)/SO(N)_\pm$ super Yang-Mills theory softly broken by a small gaugino mass. In the case of $Spin(4k)$ Yang-Mills for an integer $k\geq 2$, only two phases appear in the phase diagram, while in the $Spin(4)$ case the phase diagram contains four SPT phases protected by the $\mathbb{Z}_2\times \mathbb{Z}_2$ center symmetry. In the case of $Spin(4k+2)$ Yang-Mills for a positive integer $k$, the phase diagram contains four SPT phases protected by the $\mathbb{Z}_4$ center symmetry.

abstracts.value: Neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) uses neural networks trained on samples from the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to accelerate Boltzmann sampling. A divide-and-conquer strategy extends this approach to larger systems, but independently optimizing QAOA parameters for each subproblem is costly. In this paper, we develop a hardware-efficient implementation of neural-surrogated QeMCMC and demonstrate it using an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor. Experiments with $N=144$ binary variables reveal faster autocorrelation decay for appropriate subproblem sizes while exposing challenges in neural-surrogate learning for larger blocks. We then extend the demonstration to a system with $N=1064$, where the autocorrelation decay rate per MCMC step is approximately $5.2$ and $12.3$ times those of global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. These results demonstrate faster autocorrelation decay in a system exceeding one thousand variables using samples generated on quantum hardware.

abstracts.value: We construct a quantum measurement protocol for estimating the Rényi entanglement asymmetry, which quantifies symmetry breaking at the level of a subsystem and provides a probe of the quantum Mpemba effect. The protocol combines the SWAP test with a charge-resolving procedure based on randomized symmetry rotations. For a fixed additive accuracy $ε$, the required number of measurements scales as $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ without explicit dependence on the total system size, making the protocol particularly attractive for quantum many-body systems and lattice quantum field theories. As a representative application, we study the quantum Mpemba effect in the lattice Schwinger model with a $θ$ term using classical state-vector simulations. We further estimate the resources required to implement the protocol on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs), and a representative early-FTQC architecture. Our results provide a measurement-efficient framework for investigating anomalous symmetry-restoration dynamics in quantum many-body systems and quantum field theories.

abstracts.value: Binary neutron star (BNS) mergers excite a Kelvin--Helmholtz instability (KHI) in the shear layer between them. It is parasitized upon by the magnetic field to form a powerful magnetic dynamo. Using a large ensemble of high-resolution visco-resistive KHI-driven dynamo simulations we construct analytical, asymptotic in Reynolds number ($\rm{Re}$) models for the magnetic field growth rates and mean vertical field dynamo onset times. Our models suggest that in the $\rm{Re} \gg 1$ limit, the mean vertical field is seeded immediately, kinematic growth rates become asymptotic in $\rm{Re}$, and the dynamo moves out of the kinematic stage on $\mathcal{O}(0.1\,\rm{ms})$ timescales, readily attaining magnetar-strength fields during this transition. This suggests that most global BNS merger simulations are not time-resolving the correct KHI-driven dynamo regime.

abstracts.value: We introduce SqDMRG, which combines sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) with the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). abstracts.value: Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction (QSCI) constructs a variational determinant space from measurements of a prepared electronic state, but finite-shot sampling can repeatedly observe high-probability determinants, limiting efficient discovery of configurations important for an accurate selected-CI description. We introduce rotate--sample--unrotate (RSU) determinant discovery, in which the same state is sampled in complementary orbital frames and the observed rotated determinants generate a finite set of candidates in the canonical basis. The Hamiltonian is then diagonalized in an orthonormal selected-CI space without enumerating the full determinant space. State-targeted orbital frames are constructed from an initial selected-CI wavefunction and its external residual. For excited states, we combine RSU with the generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) to prepare target-specific sampling states. Candidate GQE circuits are evaluated by classical selected-CI diagonalization in finite sampled spaces, so the quantum procedure requires only state preparation and determinant sampling. For N$_2$, exact-state controls isolate the determinant-discovery effect: at the stretched geometry, residual-natural-orbital RSU reaches chemical accuracy with 5,000 shots, compared with 20,000 shots for conventional QSCI. The improvement persists with approximate GQE-prepared states and is also observed for target excited states. These results demonstrate improved finite-shot determinant discovery in QSCI for both ground and excited states.

titles.title: Rotated-Frame Determinant Discovery for Ground- and Excited-State Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction

abstracts.value: We present a method for efficient simulation of error propagation and decoding in universal fault-tolerant quantum circuits under stochastic Pauli noise, requiring only that the circuit has a high fault distance and that all logical non-Clifford operations are implemented by physical T, CS and CCZ gates. This is achieved using modified Pauli frame-based error tracking in which the frame contains no logical information. Decoding success is identified by verifying that the Pauli frame is still logically trivial after decoding. Using the results of Ref. [1] and the observation that the distribution of non-logical measurement outcomes in the circuit is independent of the logical state, we show that we can accurately sample all detector outcomes. Our approach can also simulate circuits containing adaptive operations conditioned on logical measurements, provided these measurements have a known outcome distribution. This applies to the majority of adaptive operations such as state teleportation and preparation by measurement. Our method only detects decoding failures and so is consistent with complexity-theoretic expectations as it cannot be used to sample from the noiseless outcome distribution of the logical circuit.

titles.title: Efficiently tracking errors and outcomes in universal quantum circuits

abstracts.value: Within the Jost-random-phase approximation (Jost-RPA), the spurious center-of-mass mode is a zero of the Jost determinant and hence a pole of the $S$ matrix. A zero at zero excitation energy $E$, whether from self-consistency or from a calibration of the residual interaction, is a pole of exactly second order when it has a single independent solution, every unoccupied bound orbital lies above the holes, and each hole is paired with every allowed partial wave; the order follows from the position of the zero, not from self-consistency. The state of this double pole, given by the Autonne-Takagi factorization of its $E^{-2}$ coefficient, is the zero-energy solution normalized by its inertia. In a self-consistent model of one energy density of the neutron and proton densities, every physical $S$-matrix element continued to $E=0$ carries the $E^{-2}$ term, contrary to an earlier conclusion. Subtracting the mode's principal part from the response changes the strength at real $E\neq0$ only through the smoothing and, in such a model, coincides with the projection of the ideal spurious state. In uncalibrated Woods-Saxon models of $^{16}$O and $^{208}$Pb the mode is a pair of poles on the imaginary axis.

abstracts.value: In the welded trees problem, an algorithm navigates a randomly labeled graph formed from two binary trees joined at their leaves through a "weld" of connecting edges. A quantum walk can navigate from root to root exponentially faster than any classical algorithm. However, recording its path destroys the constructive interference responsible for the speedup, leaving open whether some quantum algorithm can efficiently find a path between the roots. We prove that, for trees of height $n$, the quantum query complexity of finding a path between the roots with constant probability is $\tildeΘ(2^{n/3})$. This establishes an algorithmic wave-particle duality, adapting the double-slit experiment to the high-complexity regime: interference between many paths lets a quantum algorithm reach the exit efficiently, but finding a single path (the algorithmic analog of the route of a particle) requires exponentially many queries. Furthermore, the bound is tight, matching the cost of a quantum algorithm that finds collisions between paths from each root to the weld. Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle to track the information about the graph that an algorithm retains and forgets. We show that the compressed database remains close to a space of states that do not record a path between the roots by bounding the error introduced by each compressed oracle query.

titles.title: Algorithmic Wave-Particle Duality: Pathfinding in Welded Trees is Hard

abstracts.value: Causal set theory permits changes of spatial topology without the metric degeneracy that forbids them in continuum Lorentzian gravity. In four dimensions such changes enter the gravitational action only through the Gauss--Bonnet term, which is the Euler density. We show that the Euler density of a discrete space is exact, local and combinatorial: it sums to the Euler characteristic at any resolution and is supported on topological defects. The Gauss--Bonnet term of a causal set is therefore fixed rather than postulated. Because it is linear in the number of elements, which is the four-volume, it acts as a cosmological constant. Its coefficient follows without forming any functional derivative, so the known obstruction in the continuum does not arise. The everpresent cosmological constant of causal set theory assumes that the mean topological charge vanishes. We show that it does not. The species of opposite sign solves the field equations only if a positive cosmological constant is already present, and, being simply connected, it cannot carry the axion charge that supports the other species. Only one sign survives, and the sign of the cosmological term is derived rather than assumed. We recover the surviving transition from the causal order alone in every simulated sprinkling. The action of the corresponding axion wormhole then fixes the magnitude. The observed value requires an axion decay constant near the grand unification scale, and this result is insensitive to the one-loop prefactor and to the Gauss--Bonnet coupling.

titles.title: Topology change and the Gauss Bonnet term in causal set theory: the sign of the cosmological term and the axion decay constant

abstracts.value: Bounding the acceptance probabilities of quantum measurements is a recurring task in quantum information theory. An acceptance probability averaged over a random measurement setting can be bounded uniformly over the input state by the operator norm of an average of positive semidefinite operators. We prove a general inequality for such norms, valid for arbitrary finite families of positive semidefinite operators and averaging distributions. We give two applications of our operator-norm inequality. First, we determine the sharp robustness threshold for the parallel BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement game. For error thresholds $β,γ\in[0,1/2]$, when the two players may make at most $βn$ and $γn$ errors, respectively, the optimal winning probability decays exponentially if $(1-2β)^2+(1-2γ)^2>1$, tends to one exponentially fast under the reverse strict inequality, and remains bounded away from zero on the boundary. Second, we establish the achievability of every asymptotic key rate $0<R<1- 2h_2(γ)$ for one-sided device-independent BB84 quantum key distribution with tolerated bit-error rate $γ$ and asymptotically optimal reconciliation, where $h_2(\cdot)$ is the binary entropy function. Alice's measurements are trusted, while Bob may perform an arbitrary joint measurement depending on the entire basis string, subject to the protocol's receipt and isolation requirements. This recovers the usual BB84 rate in this model.

titles.title: Norm Bounds on Sums of Positive Operators with Applications to Monogamy Games and Quantum Key Distribution
